note: This summary highlights the meeting's key discussions and decisions, with direct quotes and timestamps for verification — it is not a substitute for watching the full meeting. Under this year's format, the whole School Committee sits as the Finance Committee for FY27 cost-center budget review; no votes were taken. For complete context, nuance, and anything not covered, watch the full video at the link above. (Produced by: WestbrookCurrents.com)
attendance: Present: Finance Committee Chair Noreen Poitras, School Committee Chair Andrea Mancuso, School Committee Vice Chair Katy Rice, Allison Brunette, Erin Cavallaro, Dr. Flynn Ross. Absent: Brooke Reed. City Councilor Brian McCambridge also attended.

blocks.x: Director of Music Suzanne Proulx reported a strong year: 31 students to District Honors ensembles, 11 to All-State, and 16 to the District Honors Jazz Festival.

A member flagged a roughly 25% (about $2,000) cut to the middle school's per-pupil supplies line. Staff first linked it to student counts. Later in the evening, they said it may reflect a prior-year calculation error and promised to verify.

Proulx said the middle school has already used up its instrument-repair budget this year and is borrowing from the high school's repair line. She said the cut would meaningfully affect consumables like reeds and mouthpieces.
Westbrook Performing Arts Center: Self-Sustaining, Zero General Fund Impact

Jamie Grant reported the Center remains fully self-sustaining. FY25 revenue was $193,666 against $131,561 in expenses, a $62,105 surplus. Dr. Mazjanis confirmed this has zero effect on the general fund.

Carryover funds plus Warren Memorial Foundation funding paid for a $92,000 lighting upgrade. Finance Committee Chair Noreen Poitras noted this fulfills the promise made when the Center was built roughly sixteen years ago that it would never cost taxpayers.
Energy Savings Confirmed in the Budget; Waste Removal, HVAC & High School Repairs
Director of Facilities Tony Lombardo walked through utilities and repair lines for each building. School Committee Chair Andrea Mancuso confirmed with Dr. Mazjanis the budget-level energy savings.

The overview chart projects a $302,300 drop in FY27 utility spending. Debt service (yearly loan payments) is $223,830 for solar bonding (money the City borrows and repays over years) and $256,453 for the Siemens efficiency projects, against $279,444 in projected efficiency savings.

After debt service, staff confirmed net FY27 reductions of $66,170 for solar and $22,987 for efficiency, as stated at the meeting. That is roughly $89,000 in real FY27 savings combined, expected to grow as energy prices rise.

Waste removal costs rose sharply after the district learned it was no longer covered under a municipal joint-vendor arrangement with the City. The City could supply little history, and the district has no written contract with the vendor. Lombardo negotiated a rate the vendor has verbally committed to hold for several years.
Middle school heating, ventilation and air conditioning concerns include a failing air handler and a two-year-old chiller component the vendor won't honor under warranty.

High school repairs include a $15,000 federal tree-replacement grant requiring a match, Compass program relocation costs, and roof/sidewalk safety work. Members asked whether some of these could be capital-improvement eligible, instead of paid from the operating repair budget.
“It feels like we're robbing Peter to pay Paul. We are a department of the city and we are paying the city to do work.”
blocks.cite: School Committee member Erin Cavallaro (on a $121,000 annual city charge for athletic-field maintenance)

blocks.x: “We did thoroughly explore this topic with City Hall as part of last year's budgeting process. The perspective of the municipal budgeters is that all city expenses...are assessed to the department which incurs the expense.”
blocks.cite: School Committee Chair Andrea Mancuso (on the City's rationale for the charge)

blocks.x: New Positions Requested; BusRight Parent-Tracking Rollout

Director of Transportation Melissa Foye requested two new positions. One is a van driver (cut last year, which she said has required her to personally drive long out-of-district routes). The other is a bus aide for a specific out-of-district placement.
She flagged rising bus replacement costs (now about $172,000, up from under $100,000 six years ago).

She voiced genuine safety concern about the upcoming March 27 rollout of real-time bus tracking for parents. She worried it could lead some parents to let children wait unsupervised or run toward an arriving bus.

Asked about families who need translation, staff said the district's own notice will go out translated through Reach My Teach. They said they would look into whether BusRight's messages are translated.
New Network Support Specialist Requested, Citing Cybersecurity Risk

Information technology staff member Barbara Morgan opened with a pointed message on cybersecurity. In a recent study, 52% of U.S. school districts experienced a cybersecurity incident, up from 31% two years prior. She cited a recent nearby Portland Public Schools data exposure affecting over 33,000 people.

Morgan argued the district's network currently depends on a single administrator, a “single point of failure,” and requested a new Network Support Specialist position (about $78,000). This would mean routine connection support no longer pulls the administrator away from security work. The district already effectively spends about $10,000 annually on an after-hours support stipend (extra pay for an added duty) that this position would replace.
Art Department: Two Replacement Pottery Wheels Requested

The sole new Art Department request is two replacement pottery wheels. Upper-level ceramics enrollment has grown from 3 students two years ago to 27 this year. Two of the classroom's six wheels (purchased in the late 1980s) are increasingly unreliable and raise safety concerns. The department also highlighted 2026 Maine Art Education Association recognition for two of its teachers, previously reported at the March 11 State of the Schools presentation.
Human Resources: Smallest Budget, Foundational Role

Human Resources (HR) Director Martha Sumner described a department of two: herself and a full-time HR generalist, added only two and a half years ago. The department supports 506 employees and three collective bargaining agreements (union contracts).
Sumner noted a water-heater leak at Central Office this past year damaged some HR and Finance paper records. This led to an ongoing digitization push.

Asked whether recent market-rate salary adjustments have affected staff retention, Sumner said she hasn't seen pay-driven resignations this year. Dr. Lancia said he's preparing data that appears to show a positive retention effect from the adjustments.
